title: Pizza for a Hangover: Does It Help or Make It Worse?
excerpt: Is pizza good for a hangover? What the crust, salt, and cheese do for you, when the grease backfires, why pizza works better before drinking, and leftover pizza safety.
metaDescription: Is pizza good for a hangover? How carbs and salt help, when grease makes nausea worse, why it works best before drinking, and cold leftover pizza safety.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** pizza is a middling hangover food. It isn't a cure, and it doesn't "soak up" alcohol that's already in your blood. What it does offer is a quick hit of starch to lift your energy, a decent dose of salt, and some protein from the cheese, all in a form that most people actually want to eat when they feel rough. The downside is the grease. A heavy, oily slice sits in your stomach for a long time, and if you're queasy, have heartburn, or have been throwing up, it can make you feel worse. Pizza works much better *before* a night out, when food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, than it does as a morning-after fix.

**The quick rules:** If your stomach feels settled, a slice or two of plain cheese or veggie pizza with a big glass of water is a reasonable hangover meal. Pick a thinner crust, go easy on greasy meats and hot peppers, and stop before you're stuffed. If you feel nauseous, have reflux, or vomited in the last few hours, start with fluids and something bland like toast or crackers, and save the pizza for later in the day. And if you're heading out tonight, eating pizza *before* you drink is the most useful way to use it.

> **When to see a doctor.** Most hangover stomach trouble clears up within a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for more than about a day, you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have black or tarry stools, you have severe or worsening belly pain (especially upper belly pain that spreads to your back), or you feel faint, confused, or your heart is racing and won't settle. If someone who has been drinking is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin, that can be alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away and don't leave them alone. Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that show up a day or two after you stop drinking, especially after several days of heavy drinking in a row, can be alcohol withdrawal rather than a hangover, and that also needs a doctor.

## Is Pizza Good for a Hangover? What It Actually Does

Pizza gets recommended as a hangover food mostly because it's what people crave, not because anyone has tested it. There are no clinical trials of pizza and hangovers, and there's no good evidence that any single food cures one. So the useful question is simpler: what does pizza give your body that a hungover body might want, and what does it bring that might work against you?

A hangover is a mix of several things happening at once. Researchers who study hangovers point to dehydration and mild electrolyte loss, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, an inflammatory response in the body, and sometimes low blood sugar. Some of those, food can help with a bit. Others, food can't touch.

Here's how pizza's main parts line up against that list:

| What pizza brings | How it can help | How it can backfire |
|---|---|---|
| **Starch from the crust** | Easy carbs can help bring blood sugar back up if you skipped dinner or drank a lot on an empty stomach. | A huge portion of refined carbs can leave you sluggish later. |
| **Salt from cheese, sauce, and toppings** | Helps your body hold onto the water you drink and replaces some sodium you lost. | Very salty meats can make you thirstier if you aren't also drinking water. |
| **Protein from cheese and toppings** | Keeps you full and steadies your energy for longer than plain carbs. | Not much of a downside, though cheese protein comes packaged with a lot of fat. |
| **Fat from cheese, oil, and meats** | Makes it satisfying and comforting. | Fat slows how fast your stomach empties, which can worsen nausea, bloating, and heartburn. |
| **Tomato sauce** | Small amounts of potassium and water. | Tomato is acidic and can trigger reflux in people prone to it. |

The pattern is clear. The crust, the salt, and the protein are genuinely useful on a rough morning. The grease is the part that can go wrong, and it goes wrong most for people whose stomach is already upset.

## Why You Crave Pizza When You're Hungover

If you wake up desperate for pizza, you're not imagining it, and there are a few likely reasons.

- **Your blood sugar may be low.** Alcohol interferes with the liver's ability to release stored sugar into the blood. If you drank a lot, especially without much food, you can wake up shaky, tired, and craving fast carbohydrates. A soft, doughy crust is about as fast as carbs get.
- **You want salt.** Drinking makes you pee more, and you lose some sodium along with the water. Many people find salty food especially appealing the next day.
- **Poor sleep pushes you toward rich food.** Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night's sleep, so you often wake up underslept even if you were in bed for eight hours. Studies on short sleep in general have linked it to stronger cravings for high-calorie, high-fat food.
- **Comfort and convenience.** It's warm, familiar, takes no effort, and can arrive at your door while you stay on the couch. On a hangover morning, that counts for a lot.

None of that means pizza is the *best* thing to eat. It means the craving is your body asking for carbs, salt, and calories, and pizza happens to deliver all three at once.

## Does Pizza Soak Up Alcohol?

Not in the way people imagine. Food doesn't act like a sponge that pulls alcohol back out of your system. What it does is slower and more useful, but only if the timing is right.

When there's food in your stomach, the valve at the bottom of the stomach stays closed for longer, so its contents (including alcohol) pass into your small intestine more slowly. Most alcohol gets absorbed in the small intestine. Slowing the trip there means alcohol enters your blood more gradually, so your blood alcohol level rises more slowly and peaks lower. Some of the alcohol also gets broken down in the stomach while it waits. Studies comparing drinking on an empty stomach with drinking after a meal have consistently found lower peak blood alcohol levels after eating.

The key word is *before*. Once alcohol has left your stomach and entered your blood, food can't bring it back. By the morning after, the alcohol is usually mostly or completely gone from your bloodstream. At that point, a pizza can help you feel more human, but it isn't soaking anything up. For a closer look at this myth with a different carb, see our piece on [whether bread soaks up alcohol](/never-hungover/does-bread-soak-up-alcohol).

## Eating Pizza Before Drinking: The Best Use of a Slice

If you want pizza to actually make a difference to how you feel tomorrow, eat it before your first drink. A meal with starch, protein, and fat is close to ideal for slowing alcohol absorption, and pizza happens to contain all three.

A few tips to get the most out of it:

- **Eat a real portion, not a bite.** Two or three slices, ideally with a salad or vegetables on the side, will do more than a single slice wolfed down on the way out.
- **Time it close to when you start.** Eating within an hour or so before you start drinking keeps food in your stomach during the first round, which is often when people drink fastest.
- **Don't treat it as a license.** A lower peak blood alcohol is helpful, but food won't stop you getting drunk if you keep drinking quickly. Pacing still matters more than anything you eat. Our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
- **Drink water alongside.** Pizza is salty, and salt plus alcohol plus dancing in a warm room is a fast route to thirst. Alternate alcoholic drinks with water.

If you want to compare pizza with other pre-drinking meals, our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) breaks down which foods slow absorption best.

## Late-Night Pizza After Drinking: Does It Help?

The 2 a.m. slice is a tradition for a reason, but its hangover-preventing power is limited. By the time most people stop drinking and go looking for food, much of the alcohol they drank has already been absorbed. Food at that point can slow down whatever is still in the stomach, which may take a little off the top if you were still drinking right up to the end, but it can't undo the evening.

There are some real benefits, though:

- **It can head off low blood sugar overnight.** Going to bed after heavy drinking with nothing in your stomach is a recipe for waking up shaky. A few slices of starch and protein can help.
- **The salt and a glass of water help with fluids.** If you pair your slice with a big glass of water, you go to bed less dehydrated.

And some real downsides:

- **Lying down on a full, greasy stomach invites reflux.** Alcohol relaxes the muscle at the top of your stomach that normally keeps acid down. Add a heavy, fatty meal and then lie flat, and heartburn is likely. If you're prone to it, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).
- **Very drunk people shouldn't eat a big meal.** If someone is so drunk they're stumbling, slurring heavily, or nodding off, they're at higher risk of vomiting and choking. Water and getting them safely to bed on their side matter more than food. Never let a very drunk person fall asleep on their back.
- **Late-night food safety slips.** It's easy to leave the box open on the counter and forget about it, which leads to the next problem.

The best version of late-night pizza: one or two slices, a big glass of water, then wait a little before lying down, and prop yourself up on an extra pillow if you tend to get heartburn.

## Is Cold Leftover Pizza Safe the Morning After?

Plenty of people swear by cold pizza straight out of the box the next morning. Whether it's safe depends entirely on where the box spent the night.

The USDA's general food safety advice is that perishable food shouldn't sit at room temperature for more than two hours (or one hour if it's very hot, above about 90°F). Pizza with cheese and meat toppings counts as perishable. If the box sat on the counter or the coffee table all night, the safe choice is to throw it out, even if it looks and smells fine. Bacteria that cause food poisoning don't usually change how food looks or smells, and reheating doesn't reliably fix food that has been left out too long, because some bacteria produce toxins that heat doesn't destroy.

That matters more than usual on a hangover morning. Food poisoning symptoms (nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps, diarrhea) overlap heavily with a rough hangover, so it's easy to blame the drinking for something the pizza caused, or to pile food poisoning on top of a hangover.

If you put the leftovers in the fridge within a couple of hours, they're generally fine to eat cold or reheated over the next few days. Reheating in a pan or oven tends to taste better than the microwave and can crisp up the crust, which some people find easier on the stomach than a soggy slice.

## Where Pizza Can Make a Hangover Worse

For some people on some mornings, pizza is a bad idea. Watch out for these situations.

### When you're nauseous

Fat slows down how fast your stomach empties. If you already feel sick, a meal that sits in your stomach for hours is the opposite of what you need. Start with small sips of water or an electrolyte drink, then try something bland (toast, crackers, plain rice, a banana). Once that stays down and your stomach settles, you can move on to more substantial food. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) goes through this step by step.

### When you have heartburn or reflux

Pizza has several common reflux triggers in one food: fat, acidic tomato sauce, cheese, and often spicy or fatty toppings like pepperoni. Alcohol already makes reflux more likely. If your chest is burning, pizza is probably not the move until it calms down.

### When your stomach lining is irritated

Heavy drinking can irritate the stomach lining (doctors call this gastritis), which shows up as a gnawing or burning ache in the upper belly. Rich, spicy, or acidic food can aggravate it. Blander food and time are kinder.

### When you've been vomiting

After vomiting, your stomach needs a gentle restart. Fluids first, in small amounts, then bland carbs. A greasy slice too soon is a common way to end up vomiting again.

### When you're lactose intolerant

This one is easy to forget. If dairy normally bothers you, a cheese-heavy pizza on a morning when your gut is already unsettled may bring on bloating, cramps, or diarrhea on top of the hangover.

## How to Build a Better Hangover Pizza

If your stomach can handle it and pizza is what you want, a few choices make it work better for you rather than against you.

| Choice | Better for a hangover | Harder on a hangover |
|---|---|---|
| **Crust** | Thin or regular crust | Deep dish, stuffed crust, extra-oily pan crust |
| **Cheese** | Normal amount | Extra cheese, cheese-stuffed crust |
| **Toppings** | Plain cheese, vegetables, chicken, ham | Pepperoni, sausage, bacon, heaps of meat |
| **Heat** | Mild | Hot peppers, chili flakes, spicy sauces |
| **Sauce** | Regular tomato or a white sauce if tomato triggers reflux | Extra sauce if you have heartburn |
| **Portion** | One or two slices, then wait | Half a large pizza in one sitting |
| **Drink** | Water or an electrolyte drink | More alcohol, extra-large soda |

A few more practical tips:

- **Blot the grease.** Pressing a napkin on top of a slice removes some of the surface oil. It won't turn pizza into health food, but it can make it a bit easier to digest.
- **Add something fresh.** A side salad or some fruit adds water, potassium, and fiber without much effort.
- **Pair it with fluids.** Pizza's salt helps your body hold onto water, but only if you drink some. A big glass of water with the meal is the single best upgrade.
- **Eat slowly and stop early.** A hungover stomach is easily overwhelmed. Eat a slice, wait ten or fifteen minutes, and see how you feel before reaching for the next.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog" beer with it.** More alcohol only postpones the hangover, and there's no good evidence that it helps.

## Pizza vs. Other Hangover Foods

Pizza isn't the only option, and it's worth knowing how it compares. Here's a rough guide.

| Food | What it offers | Main drawback |
|---|---|---|
| **Pizza** | Carbs, salt, protein, comfort | Greasy; can worsen nausea and reflux |
| **Eggs and toast** | Protein, easy carbs, gentle on most stomachs | Less exciting when you're craving something rich |
| **Toast or crackers** | Bland, easy carbs, good first food | Very little protein or salt on their own |
| **Banana** | Easy carbs, potassium, gentle | Not filling on its own |
| **Broth or soup** | Fluids and salt together | Light; you'll want more later |
| **Burger and fries** | Carbs, salt, protein | Even greasier than most pizza |
| **Oatmeal** | Slow-release carbs, gentle | Bland, needs time to prepare |

In short, pizza is roughly in the same category as other comfort fast food: fine if your stomach is fine, not ideal if it isn't. Eggs and toast give you most of the same benefits with less grease, and our piece on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why they come up so often. For the full picture across many foods, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover), and for more on grease specifically, our article on [greasy food and hangovers](/never-hungover/greasy-food-hangover).

## What a Hangover Actually Needs

Food is only one piece. However good your slice, the things that matter most for a hangover are not on the menu.

1. **Fluids.** Drink water steadily through the morning. If you were sick or sweated a lot, an electrolyte drink or an oral rehydration solution can help replace salts as well as water.
2. **Time.** The symptoms of a hangover usually peak around when your blood alcohol returns to zero and then fade over the day. Nothing reliably speeds that up.
3. **Rest.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, so a nap or an early night often does more than any food.
4. **Gentle food when you're ready.** Something with carbs to steady blood sugar, some protein, and some salt. Pizza fits, as long as your stomach agrees.
5. **Careful pain relief, if any.** If you reach for a painkiller, follow the label, take it with food, and know that acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol need extra care. Ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate an already upset stomach.

There is no good evidence that any food, drink, or pill cures a hangover once you have one. What you can do is support your body while it recovers, and take steps beforehand to make the next one milder.

## Who Should Skip Pizza the Morning After

Pizza is a poor choice for a hangover morning if you:

- Feel nauseous or have vomited in the last few hours
- Have frequent heartburn, acid reflux, or have been told you have GERD
- Have an upper-belly ache that feels burning or gnawing
- Are lactose intolerant or sensitive to dairy
- Have a gallbladder problem, since heavy, fatty meals can trigger gallbladder pain
- Have been told by a doctor to limit salt, for example because of high blood pressure, heart failure, or kidney disease

If any of those apply, start with fluids and something bland, and see how you feel. Pizza will still be there tomorrow.

## A Note on Making the Next Morning Easier

If you notice you're ordering hangover pizza most weekends, the most effective changes happen the night before rather than the morning after: eat a proper meal before you start, pace your drinks, alternate with water, and know when to call it a night.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, and the human evidence is still limited, so it's promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers outright, and it doesn't replace eating, hydrating, and drinking less. If you'd like to try it alongside those habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly.

## The Bottom Line

- Pizza isn't a hangover cure, and it doesn't soak up alcohol that's already in your blood.
- Its crust, salt, and cheese can help with low energy, low blood sugar, and salt loss, especially paired with plenty of water.
- Its grease can make nausea, heartburn, and an irritated stomach worse, so skip it if you feel queasy or have been sick.
- It does the most good *before* drinking, when food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed and lowers your peak.
- Late-night pizza is fine in moderation, but drink water with it and don't lie flat straight after.
- Throw out pizza that sat out overnight. Food poisoning on top of a hangover is a miserable combination.
- If your stomach symptoms are severe, include blood, or won't settle after a day, see a doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is pizza good for a hangover?**

It can be a reasonable hangover meal if your stomach feels settled. The crust gives you easy carbs, the cheese adds protein, and the salt helps your body hold onto the water you drink. But the grease can make nausea and heartburn worse, so if you feel queasy, start with fluids and bland food instead. Pizza isn't a cure, and there's no good evidence that any food cures a hangover.

**Does pizza soak up alcohol?**

No, not once the alcohol is in your blood. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol passes into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed, which lowers your peak blood alcohol. That only helps if you eat before or while drinking. The morning after, there's nothing left in your stomach for pizza to absorb.

**Should I eat pizza before drinking?**

Yes, pizza is a decent pre-drinking meal. It combines starch, protein, and fat, which together slow alcohol absorption and help keep your blood alcohol from spiking. Eat a proper portion within an hour or so of your first drink, add vegetables if you can, and still pace yourself and alternate with water, because food won't stop you getting drunk if you drink quickly.

**Is it bad to eat pizza when you're drunk?**

A slice or two with a big glass of water is generally fine and can help prevent low blood sugar overnight. Avoid eating a huge, greasy meal right before lying down, because alcohol and fat together make reflux more likely. Someone who is very drunk, stumbling, or nodding off shouldn't be given a big meal, because they're at higher risk of vomiting and choking. Get them to bed on their side and watch for signs of alcohol poisoning.

**Is cold pizza left out overnight safe to eat with a hangover?**

The safe answer is no. USDA food safety guidance says perishable food shouldn't sit at room temperature for more than two hours. Pizza left out all night should be thrown out, even if it looks and smells fine, because reheating doesn't reliably make it safe. Pizza that went into the fridge within a couple of hours is fine to eat cold or reheated over the next few days.

**What kind of pizza is best for a hangover?**

A thin or regular crust with plain cheese or vegetable toppings is the easiest on a hungover stomach. Go easy on pepperoni, sausage, extra cheese, and hot peppers, which add grease and can trigger heartburn. Blot surface oil with a napkin, eat slowly, and drink a big glass of water with it.

**Why do I crave pizza when I'm hungover?**

Alcohol can lower your blood sugar, make you lose salt and water, and disrupt your sleep. All three push your appetite toward fast carbs, salty food, and rich, high-calorie meals. Pizza delivers all of those at once, which is why it's such a common craving. The craving is real, but it doesn't mean pizza is the best food for recovery.

**Is pizza or a greasy breakfast better for a hangover?**

They're in a similar category. Both offer carbs, salt, and protein, and both can be hard on a nauseous or reflux-prone stomach because of the fat. If your stomach is fine, either is okay in a sensible portion. If it isn't, eggs on toast, a banana, or broth are gentler places to start.
